analysis.one_liner: Restricts employers from letting algorithms make or dominate hiring, firing, pay, and scheduling decisions about workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2026 and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put limits on employers that use software and artificial intelligence to make decisions about workers. It would stop employers from relying mainly on an automated system to hire, fire, discipline, schedule, or set pay, and require them to tell workers how the system works and give them a way to appeal. Workers could opt out and ask to be evaluated or managed by a human. It would also require companies that build and use workplace AI to test it for bias and other harms before deploying it, report annually on its effects, and face fines and lawsuits if they violate the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers with 11 or more workers, including gig and contract workers performing work for remuneration. They would get the right to a human decision-maker instead of an algorithm, a plain-language explanation of how automated systems evaluate them, at least 7 days' notice before an algorithm-driven firing or discipline, an appeals process, protection from retaliation, and the ability to sue or join a class action instead of being forced into arbitration [S2]. Unions would gain a say, since employers must bargain over decisions to implement such systems [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Employers could no longer rely predominantly on an automated decision system to hire, fire, discipline, schedule, or set pay — a human decision-maker would have to be in the loop [S2].
Workers and applicants could opt out of being managed or screened by an algorithm and request a human instead, including when a third-party vendor does the screening [S2].

Before any adverse action taken with help from an algorithm — firing, discipline, demotion, cut hours, worse schedules — the employer must disclose how the system works and give the worker at least 7 days' notice [S2].

Developers and employers must test workplace AI for discrimination and risks to workers' rights before deploying it, reassess it every year, and publish a summary; an oversight office at the Department of Labor receives the reports and can investigate [S2].

The bill bans forced arbitration and class-action waivers for these claims, lets workers sue with attorney's fees, and protects workers who refuse to follow an algorithm's output when exercising their own judgment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers using automated decision systems for hiring, management, or scheduling — large retailers, logistics and warehouse operators, gig platforms, and the vendors selling them such systems — would bear the cost of disclosures, predeployment evaluations, annual impact assessments, training, and potential statutory damages of up to $40,000 per violation [S2]. Some of that compliance cost could be passed to consumers or slow adoption of management software [S2].

drawbacks.text: Employers would face real compliance costs: predeployment evaluations, annual impact assessments, published summaries, 10-year record retention, and training for anyone operating the systems [S2].
Small employers are exempt — the rules only cover employers with 11 or more covered individuals, so workers at the smallest businesses get no protection [S2].
Companies may redact trade secrets from the public summaries of their evaluations, so the public record of how an algorithm works would not always be complete [S2].

Opponents of workplace AI rules generally argue that disclosure, testing, and certification requirements slow down technology adoption and add legal exposure; this bill imposes both on any employer using automated hiring or management tools, and adds statutory damages of $5,000-$20,000 per violation (up to $40,000 for willful or repeat violations) [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — a human in the loop, explanations, appeals, and enforceable penalties for algorithmic firing and scheduling — directly address documented harms of workplace AI. The costs are real: employers selling to consumers or governments may face higher costs and slower decisions, and some firms might hire fewer workers or shift hiring abroad to avoid the rules. The bill's design mitigates the classic transparency-burden objection by letting companies redact trade secrets [S2], and by phasing in assessments for systems built before enactment. The main honest criticism is enforcement scope: a 7-day notice requirement before an adverse action helps, but companies could still time automated decisions to squeeze workers within legal limits, and small employers with 10 or fewer workers are exempt [S2].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and with no further action on the record it sits there while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the No Robot Bosses Act on June 18, 2026, joined by six other senators, all Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that referral is the last action in the record [S4].

The bill would bar employers from relying predominantly on an automated decision system for hiring, firing, discipline, scheduling, or pay decisions, require disclosure of how such systems work, and give workers a right to opt out of algorithmic management and application screening in favor of a human [S2].

It would require developers and employers to run and publish predeployment and annual impact assessments of workplace AI, create a Fairness and Transparency Office at the Department of Labor to enforce the rules, and ban predispute arbitration and class-action waivers for claims under the bill [S2].

Enforcement includes a private right of action with statutory damages from $5,000 to $40,000 per violation, whistleblower protection for workers who refuse to follow an algorithm's output, and enforcement by state attorneys general [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers using or selling algorithmic management tools are better off so far: no committee action means no obligations have been imposed, and they keep operating under current law.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was read twice and referred to the HELP Committee [S1].

for.name: Sens. Schatz, Sanders, Baldwin, Warren, Blumenthal, and Fetterman

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the bill sits in a Senate committee with no action [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Employers using algorithmic management and AI hiring tools (retail, logistics, gig platforms, staffing, large service chains)
industries.note: They would have to keep a human in the loop, disclose how their systems work, run predeployment and annual assessments, and face statutory damages and lawsuits when the software drives firings or discipline. Their interest in keeping cheap, opaque algorithmic management runs against workers' interest in appealable, human-reviewed decisions.

industries.industry: Vendors of workplace AI and automated decision systems (HR tech, scheduling and productivity-scoring software)
industries.note: Developers would face predeployment evaluations, usage limits, and shared legal responsibility for how employers use their products, including a ban on knowingly selling them for uses outside the tested purposes. Their interest in unregulated sales runs against workers' interest in tested systems.

The bill does not ban workplace AI; it channels decisions through it with human oversight, mandatory training, and documentation, effectively institutionalizing automated decision systems as a permanent part of management under new rules.

analysis.trajectory: Bills of this type typically stall in committee without a hearing or markup. With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action in the record, and the 119th Congress ending in January 2027, the most likely path is that the bill dies in committee without a floor vote unless the sponsor uses it to build a record or attaches provisions to a larger package.
